entry: Ancient astronomical instrument, a star chart and physical model of the visible half-dome of the sky. In its simplest form it is a metal disc with wires, cutouts and perforations that allow astronomical positions to be calculated. It measures the altitude of a celestial body above the [[Horizon]], identifies stars or planets, and determines latitude from local time. It was used in [[Classical antiquity|classical antiquity]], the [[Byzantine Empire]], the [[Islamic Golden Age]], the [[Middle Ages|European Middle Ages]] and the [[Age of Discovery]]. The astrolabe was a precursor to the [[Sextant|sextant]].

One of twelve 30° divisions of the [[Zodiac|zodiac]] used in Western astrology. The signs are enumerated from the vernal [[Equinox|equinox]], the First Point of Aries, and include Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius and Pisces. Each sign was named after a [[Constellation|constellation]] through which the [[Sun]] annually moved, but axial precession has shifted the divisions out of alignment with those constellations. Scientific astronomy used the same sectors of the [[Ecliptic|ecliptic]] until the 19th century.

Range of divinatory practices based on the apparent positions of celestial objects, recognized as [[Pseudoscience|pseudoscientific]] since the 18th century. Forms of astrology have been practiced since at least the 2nd millennium BCE, originating in calendrical systems used to predict seasonal change. Western astrology traces its roots to Mesopotamia and spread to [[Ancient Greece]], Rome, the Islamic world and Europe. Contemporary Western astrology is often associated with horoscopes that purport to explain personality and predict events in a person's life. Before the Enlightenment it was a scholarly tradition, closely related to [[Astronomy|astronomy]], meteorology, medicine and [[Alchemy|alchemy]]. Since the late 19th century, researchers have found astrology to have no scientific validity or explanatory power.

Branch of [[Astronomy|astronomy]] concerned with the precise measurement of the positions and movements of stars and other celestial bodies. It provides the kinematics and physical origin of the Solar System and the Milky Way. Its history is tied to star catalogues. Around 190 BC [[Hipparchus]] used the catalogue of his predecessors to discover Earth's precession, and he developed the brightness scale still in use. In the 16th century [[Tycho Brahe]] measured star positions with a precision of 15–35 arcsec. Friedrich Bessel, the father of modern astrometry, made the first measurement of stellar [[Parallax|parallax]], for the [[Binary star|binary star]] 61 Cygni. In the 1980s [[Charge-coupled device|charge-coupled devices]] replaced photographic plates and reduced optical uncertainties to one milliarcsecond. The [[European Space Agency]]'s Hipparcos satellite, operated from 1989 to 1993, took astrometry into orbit.

Person trained, equipped and deployed by a human spaceflight program to serve as a commander or crew member of a [[Spacecraft|spacecraft]]. The word, from [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] roots meaning “star” and “sailor,” is generally reserved for professional space travelers, though it is sometimes applied to anyone who has flown into space. In the United States it is a designated term used by [[NASA]], the Federal Aviation Administration and the military, each with slightly different criteria. As of April 2026, 781 humans had flown in space, and over 290 individuals had visited the [[International Space Station]]. The suborbital flight of the privately funded SpaceShipOne in 2004 created the category of commercial astronaut.

System of reference frames for specifying the positions of celestial objects on the [[Celestial sphere|celestial sphere]]. Spherical coordinates are analogous to the [[Geographic coordinate system|geographic coordinate system]] used on Earth, and the systems differ in their choice of fundamental plane. The horizontal, or altitude-azimuth, system is based on an observer's position and the [[Horizon]], so an object's position changes with time. The [[Equatorial coordinate system|equatorial system]] is fixed relative to the celestial poles and the March equinox and is the normal system for most professional astronomers. The [[Ecliptic]] system uses the plane of Earth's orbit and was used to define the twelve [[Astrological sign|astrological signs]] of the zodiac. Modern star maps almost exclusively use equatorial coordinates.

Naturally occurring physical entity, association or structure that exists within the universe. In astronomy the terms object and body are often used interchangeably, but a body is a single, tightly bound physical object, such as an [[Asteroid]], moon, planet or star, whereas an object may be a looser structure, such as a [[Planetary system]], [[Star cluster]] or [[Nebula]]. A [[Comet]] is both: its frozen nucleus is a body, and the whole comet, with its diffuse coma and tail, is an object. Early cultures regarded these bodies as deities. In 1543 [[Nicolaus Copernicus]] published a heliocentric model placing the Sun at the center of the [[Solar System]]. In 1610 [[Galileo Galilei|Galileo]] observed the four largest moons of Jupiter, now named the Galilean moons.

Unit of length defined as 149,597,870,700 m, used primarily for distances within the [[Solar System]] or around other stars. Historically it was conceived as the average distance between [[Earth]] and the [[Sun]], before its modern redefinition in 2012. Its value is based on the semi-major axis of Earth's orbit. One au is approximately equivalent to 499 light-seconds, and it is a fundamental component of the [[Parsec|parsec]]. In 1976 the International Astronomical Union (IAU) defined the unit through the Gaussian gravitational constant. In 2012 the IAU fixed it as a conventional value matching the meter and recommended the symbol au.

Branch of [[Astronomy|astronomy]] applying the methods and principles of physics and chemistry to the study of celestial objects and phenomena. Subjects include the Sun, other stars, [[Galaxy|galaxies]], extrasolar planets, the interstellar medium and the [[Cosmic microwave background|cosmic microwave background]]. Emissions are examined across the [[Electromagnetic spectrum|electromagnetic spectrum]], and the properties studied include luminosity, density, temperature and chemical composition. Research covers [[Dark matter]], [[Dark energy]], [[Black hole|black holes]], and the origin and ultimate fate of the universe. The field developed from spectroscopy: by 1860 [[Gustav Kirchhoff]] and the chemist Robert Bunsen showed that dark lines in the solar spectrum matched bright lines of known gases, proving that the elements in the Sun and stars were also found on Earth.

Autonomous community in northwestern [[Spain]], coextensive with the province of Asturias. It contains part of the territory of the medieval Kingdom of Asturias and has a population of about 1 million. The capital is Oviedo, and Gijón is the largest city and main seaport. The region has a maritime climate, with abundant rain and mild winters. The Romans under [[Augustus]] took the region in 29–19 BC, but the Astures were never fully conquered. [[Cider]] and [[Cheese|cheese]] remain important to regional identity.

City (pop., 2022: 462,241), capital and largest city of [[Paraguay]], on the eastern bank of the Paraguay River. It is one of the oldest cities in South America and is known as the “Mother of Cities” because Spanish expeditions from it founded other cities, including the second foundation of [[Buenos Aires]]. Its [[Metropolitan area|metropolitan area]] exceeds 2.3 million inhabitants and concentrates 70% of national GDP. The city houses the national government's three branches, including the [[Executive (government)|executive]], and is the headquarters of the Permanent Review Court of Mercosur. It will host the 2031 Pan American Games.

City in Upper [[Egypt]], capital of Aswan Governorate, on the east bank of the [[Nile]] at the First Cataract. It is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities, with a recorded history of more than 2,600 years. In antiquity it was the southern frontier of [[Ancient Egypt]], and its [[Granite|granite]] quarries supplied monuments throughout Egypt; the quarries still operate. Five monuments within the UNESCO [[World Heritage Site]] of the Nubian Monuments are in the city, including the Old and Middle Kingdom tombs of Qubbet el-Hawa. The Nubian Museum holds finds from the campaign to save monuments of [[Nubia|Lower Nubia]] before the [[Aswan High Dam|Aswan Dam]] flooded the area. Aswan is considered a global tourist winter destination.

Embankment dam across the Nile at [[Aswan]], Egypt, one of the world's largest. Built between 1960 and 1970 with help from the [[Soviet Union]], it was designed to control [[Flood|floods]], increase water storage for [[Irrigation|irrigation]] and generate [[Hydroelectricity|hydroelectricity]]. It was seen as pivotal to Egypt's industrialization and, when completed, was the tallest earthen dam in the world. It created Lake Nasser. The earlier Low Dam, completed in 1902, had too small a capacity to stop floods and droughts, which could destroy crops or cause [[Famine|famine]]. The High Dam allowed floods to be controlled and water to be stored for release over several years, protecting the [[Cotton|cotton]] crop. Planning followed the overthrow of the monarchy by the Free Officers Movement, including [[Gamal Abdel Nasser]].

Desert [[Plateau|plateau]] along the Pacific coast of South America, in northern [[Chile]], covering about 105,000 sq km. It is the driest nonpolar desert in the world and the largest [[Fog|fog]] desert. Average rainfall is about 15 mm (0.6 in) a year, and some locations receive only 1 to 3 mm. Aridity results from a constant temperature inversion caused by the cool Humboldt Current and a strong Pacific anticyclone, and from a two-sided rain shadow between the [[Andes]] and the Chilean Coast Range. The desert has been used to simulate expeditions to [[Mars]]. Its dry, stable air makes it a leading site for ground-based [[Observatory|astronomy]], and the region has large [[Copper|copper]] mines.

Interferometer of 66 [[Radio telescope|radio telescopes]] in the [[Atacama Desert]] of northern [[Chile]], observing millimeter and submillimeter [[Wavelength|wavelengths]]. It was built on the Chajnantor plateau at 5,000 m, chosen for its high elevation and low [[Humidity|humidity]], which reduce noise and signal attenuation from Earth's atmosphere. The antennas can be moved over distances from 150 m to 16 km, giving the array a variable zoom, and most of its sensitivity comes from the large number of dishes. It is an international partnership among [[Europe]], the [[United States]], Canada, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Chile. Costing about US$1.4 billion, it is the most expensive ground-based telescope in operation. Observations began in 2011, and the array has been fully operational since March 2013.

Last effective [[Inca Empire|Inca]] emperor, reigning from April 1532 until his capture and execution during the [[Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire|Spanish conquest]]. He was a son of the emperor Huayna Cápac and was governor of [[Quito]] under his half-brother Huáscar, who had become emperor. From 1529 to 1532 they contested the succession in the Inca Civil War, and Atahualpa defeated Huáscar's forces and took him prisoner. In November 1532 [[Francisco Pizarro]] and his Spanish force captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca. In captivity he offered a ransom, but the Spanish then tried him for treason and for the murder of Huáscar. He was sentenced to burning at the stake, but after his baptism he was garroted instead. His execution accelerated the collapse of centralized Inca authority.

Indian statesman and poet, prime minister of India in 1996 and from 1998 to 2004. He was the first non-Congress prime minister to serve a full term. A co-founder and senior leader of the [[Bharatiya Janata Party]] (BJP), he had been a volunteer of the [[Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh]]. He was elected to the *Lok Sabha* ten times over five decades. As prime minister he authorized the Pokhran-II nuclear tests in 1998, traveled to Lahore by bus to meet Nawaz Sharif, and after the [[Kargil War]] invited Pervez Musharraf to a summit at [[Agra]]. His government pursued economic reforms, including privatization and encouragement of foreign investment. He received the *Bharat Ratna*, India's highest civilian honor.

Neurological sign of lack of voluntary coordination of muscle movements, indicating dysfunction of parts of the [[Nervous system|nervous system]], such as the [[Cerebellum]]. It can affect gait, speech and eye movements, and may be limited to one side of the body, a condition called hemiataxia. Cerebellar ataxia causes poor balance, a widened-base gait and irregular, uncoordinated movements. Acquired ataxia can result from [[Stroke|stroke]] or [[Multiple sclerosis|multiple sclerosis]]. Treatment focuses on [[Physical therapy|physical therapy]] to improve strength and balance, and most hereditary ataxias have no cure.

Egyptian Christian theologian and 20th patriarch of [[Alexandria]], serving from 328 to 373. As a deacon and assistant to Bishop Alexander, he took a leading role against [[Arius]] and Arianism at the [[First Council of Nicaea]] in 325. He succeeded Alexander as patriarch and faced repeated conflict with the Arians and with successive Roman emperors, which led to five exiles totaling 17 years. His anti-Arian polemics, *On the Incarnation* and a biography of Saint Anthony the Great are among his notable writings. He is venerated as a saint in the [[Catholic Church]] and [[Eastern Orthodox Church|Eastern Orthodox Church]], and is traditionally honored as one of the four Great Greek Church Fathers. His efforts earned him the title “Father of Orthodoxy.”

Ancient Greek goddess of wisdom, warfare and handicraft, later syncretized with the Roman goddess Minerva. She was the patron of [[Athens]], which most likely gave her its name, and her temples usually stood atop the city's acropolis; the [[Parthenon]] is dedicated to her. Her symbols include owls, [[Olive|olive]] trees and snakes. In myth she was born from the forehead of Zeus, and she won the patronage of Athens from Poseidon by creating the first olive tree. Along with Aphrodite and Hera, she was one of three goddesses whose feud resulted in the [[Trojan War]]. In the *Iliad* she assists the Achaeans, and in the *Odyssey* she is the tutelary deity of Odysseus. Since the [[Renaissance]] she has been an international symbol of wisdom, the arts and classical learning.

City (pop., 2021: 643,452), capital of [[Greece]] and of the Attica region. It is one of the world's oldest cities, with a recorded history spanning over 3,400 years. [[Classical Athens]] was a powerful city-state and a center of ancient democracy, the arts and philosophy. Its urban area numbers over 3.6 million, and Athens is the southernmost capital on the European mainland. The [[Parthenon]] on the [[Acropolis of Athens|Acropolis]] is considered a key landmark of early Western culture. Athens is classified as a Beta (+) [[Global city|global city]], and its port Piraeus is the second-busiest passenger port in Europe. The city hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896 and the 2004 Summer [[Olympic Games|Olympics]].

Chronic inflammatory disease involving the buildup of atheromatous plaques in the walls of [[Artery|arteries]], driven by elevated blood levels of [[Cholesterol|cholesterol]], primarily LDL. Plaque is made of fat, cholesterol, immune cells and calcium, and narrows arteries, limiting the flow of oxygen-rich blood. The disease is typically asymptomatic for decades and can lead to [[Coronary artery disease]], [[Stroke]] or peripheral artery disease. Risk factors include abnormal cholesterol levels, high [[Blood pressure|blood pressure]], [[Diabetes]], [[Smoking|smoking]] and [[Obesity]]. It is a leading cause of death and disability in developed countries.

City (pop., 2020: 498,715), capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]]. Situated in the foothills of the [[Appalachian Mountains]], it has the densest urban tree coverage of any major U.S. city. Atlanta was founded as the terminus of the state-sponsored Western and Atlantic Railroad, which gave it its name. It was captured in 1864 during the [[American Civil War]] and was almost entirely burned under Union general William T. Sherman. In the 1950s and 1960s it was a major organizing center of the [[Civil rights movement|civil rights movement]], with [[Martin Luther King Jr.]] among its leaders. Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport has been the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic since 1998, except in 2020. The economy spans transportation, aerospace, [[Logistics|logistics]], healthcare, media and [[Information technology|information technology]]. The [[Gentrification|gentrification]] of some neighborhoods has intensified with the Atlanta Beltline rail trail.

Annual period, June 1–November 30, covering most tropical cyclone formation in the North [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]]. The dates are a convention, and cyclogenesis can occur at any time of year. Peak activity falls from late August to September. On average a season has 14 named storms, of which 7 become hurricanes and 3 become major hurricanes, Category 3 or higher on the [[Saffir–Simpson scale]]. The most active season on record was 2020, with 30 named [[Tropical cyclone|tropical cyclones]]; the 2005 season had more hurricanes, with a record 15. The least active was 1914, with one known tropical cyclone.

Trade in enslaved Africans carried by slave ships from Europe and the [[New World]] to the [[Americas]], from the 16th century into the 19th. Most of those transported were from [[Central Africa|Central]] and [[West Africa]] and were bought from African merchants. Portuguese traders built barracoons at African slaving bases to gather captives for the next ship, while northern European traders used their own ships as bases on the coast. The enslaved worked on coffee, tobacco, cocoa, sugar and cotton plantations, and in mines. By the mid-17th century English colonies had a racial [[Caste|caste]] system of chattel slavery. About 12.75 million Africans were loaded onto slave ships, and up to 2 million died during the voyage. Several governments banned the trade near the start of the 19th century, though smuggling continued.
